name: Dorsal hump rasping (DIY)

lead: Dorsal hump rasping is the do-it-yourself attempt to flatten a bump on the bridge of the nose by filing or striking it. The payoff people want is a straighter, smoother side profile without paying for surgery.

The idea is that repeated filing or impact reduces the bone and cartilage of the bump. Reference sources describe hump reduction only as part of rhinoplasty, where a surgeon reshapes the bump with instruments under anesthesia and the nose is then taped and splinted while it heals. No published study or reliable source describes a home method, and the wiki's sources do not document how common it is.

paras: Posters who discuss it describe working on the bump themselves at home, without a surgeon. No published routine or timeline exists. The surgical version it imitates is followed by a dressing and splint, and swelling can take a year or more to settle fully.

The nasal bones and cartilage support breathing as well as shape. Injury, infection, airway problems and an uneven result are general concerns with any trauma to the nose, and no study evaluates the home practice. Anyone wanting a lower bridge can ask a facial plastic surgeon about rhinoplasty.

chain: Home filing or striking of bump
angle.text: The goal is a flatter, smoother nasal bridge without surgery. People who try it file or strike the bump at home, expecting the bone to wear down. Surgical sources describe hump reduction only as a surgeon-performed procedure.

lead: Dorsal hump rasping (DIY) is the name given to attempts to lower a bump on the nasal bridge at home by filing or striking it, with the goal of a straighter nose profile without paying for surgery. The bridge of the nose is one of the most visible profile features, and a smoother line from brow to tip is what people seeking this are after.[1]

In professional practice, hump reduction is a step of rhinoplasty: the surgeon cuts the cartilage portion with a scalpel and chisels the bony portion with an osteotome, and then smooths the cut bone with rasps of various grades.[1] The home practice borrows the rasping step; the sources consulted do not document how common it is.

After surgery the nose is taped and fitted with a protective splint, the dressing is typically removed after about a week, and swelling can take at least a year to settle.[1] Rhinoplasty references list named complications such as pollybeak, saddle nose, inverted-V, rocker and open roof deformity, and report that revision is needed in roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases.[1] No study evaluates self-performed hump reduction.

paras: Rhinoplasty references describe surgeon-performed reshaping: cartilage is cut with a scalpel, bone is chiselled with an osteotome and the cut bone is sculpted and smoothed with rasps.[1] The nose is then taped and splinted, with the dressing typically removed about a week later.[1] Recovery involves prolonged swelling, and healing varies between individuals.[1]

Rhinoplasty references say results can be unpredictable, that revision surgery is needed in roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases, and that smoking impairs healing.[1] Named contour problems after surgical hump reduction include open roof, inverted-V and saddle nose deformities.[1] Facial feminization surgery references note that reducing nasal size carries a risk of impairing nasal valve function, which relates to breathing.[2] No study evaluates outcomes or injuries from self-performed filing or striking.
